---
title: "The models"
---

MINTverse ships four trained models. Three are gradient-boosted trees in `estimint` that
convert between transmission quantities, and one is a sequence model in `stateMINT` that
produces trajectories. Nothing is fitted, tuned or configured at call time. All you
choose is which model to call and what to put in.

## The three estiMINT conversions

Each of the three answers one question. All three share the same six covariates
describing the setting (`dn0_use`, `Q0`, `phi_bednets`, `seasonal`, `itn_use` and
`irs_use`), plus the quantity being converted.

| Name | Extra input | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `"prevalence"` | `prev_y9` | EIR |
| `"hbr"` | `hbr_y9` | EIR |
| `"eir_to_hbr"` | `eir` | HBR |

`load_xgb_model` returns a dictionary rather than a bare booster, because the booster is
only part of the estimator.

```{python}
from estimint import load_xgb_model

model = load_xgb_model("prevalence")

print("features   ", model["features"])
print("transform  ", model["preprocess"]["transform"], "->", model["preprocess"]["inverse"])
print("calibrator ", model["calibrator"]["kind"])
print("rounds     ", model["best_nrounds"])
```

Three things in that output explain the behaviour of `run_xgb_model`. The first is that
the target is `log10`. EIR spans several orders of magnitude, and on the raw scale
squared error would be dominated entirely by the high-transmission rows while the low end
was fitted as noise. Training against $\log_{10}(\mathrm{EIR})$ makes the loss relative,
so a factor-of-two error costs the same at EIR 2 as at EIR 200. `run_xgb_model` inverts
the transform (`pow10`) before returning, so you always get an EIR in natural units.

The second is a quantile-mapping calibrator that sits after the booster. It is there
because a boosted-tree ensemble regresses towards the mean. Its predictions come out
compressed relative to the truth, and the compression is greatest in the tails, where the
extreme settings are. Quantile mapping corrects the marginal distribution of predictions
back onto the distribution of the training targets, restoring the spread that the loss
function shrank.

The third is a monotone smoothing pass over the result. Trees are piecewise-constant. A
raw booster predicting EIR from prevalence produces a staircase, flat over a range of
prevalences and then a step, and it can also be locally non-monotone, so that a slightly
higher prevalence maps to a slightly lower EIR. That is physically wrong, and it prevents
any reliable inversion or optimisation against the model. The smoothing pass enforces
monotonicity along the input being converted.

The calibration and the smoothing are baked into the fitted artefact rather than applied
batch-wise across whatever rows you happen to pass. A single-row query therefore still
lands on a smooth, monotone curve. You can call the model one row at a time, in any
order. Sweep prevalence from 0.05 to 0.75 and the resulting EIRs rise monotonically, on a
curve rather than a staircase.

The models are bundled inside the wheel. Nothing is downloaded, and `load_xgb_model` is a
local file read.

## The stateMINT emulator

`stateMINT` is a Mamba2 state-space model, implemented in JAX and Flax and trained to
reproduce [`malariasimulation`](https://mrc-ide.github.io/malariasimulation/). It takes a
setting and a campaign and returns 157 steps of prevalence, or 157 steps of cases.

The architecture is stored in the artefact and can be read back.

```{python}
from stateMINT.model import Mamba2Regressor

artifact = Mamba2Regressor.from_pretrained(
    "dide-ic/stateMINT", predictor="prevalence", revision="v1.2.2",
)

for key, value in artifact.model_config.items():
    print(f"{key:<12} {value}")
```

The configuration is two layers, `d_model` 256, `d_state` 128, and 16 input channels per
timestep. The 16 channels are the twelve static covariates, with the `after_intervention`
ones switched on at day 3285, plus four derived time channels that `prepare_inputs`
builds. It is a small model by current standards, which is why it runs comfortably on a
CPU.

`from_pretrained` returns a **`ModelArtifact`** rather than a `Mamba2Regressor`, so the
network itself is `artifact.model`. The artefact bundles it with the scaler and the two
config dictionaries. A set of weights without its scaler is useless. `predictor` is baked
into the checkpoint, and prevalence and cases are two separately trained models with
separate scalers. Loading the wrong one returns a prediction for the other quantity,
without any error being raised.

### Causality

The model is **causal**, so the prediction at step $t$ depends only on the inputs at
steps $1 \dots t$ and never on anything later. The architecture enforces this rather than
leaving the training to learn it. Prevalence in the second year after a campaign cannot
be influenced by what happens in the third.

Causality is what makes the pre-campaign baseline meaningful. The `after_intervention`
covariates are zero for every step before day 3285, and the model cannot see forward, so
the first 78 steps of a trajectory are computed as though no campaign were coming. Two
scenarios that differ only in their campaign share an identical baseline, so any
difference between their curves is the campaign.

### Model space and natural units

Prevalence is trained in **logit** space and cases in **log1p** space. Both transforms
exist because the raw targets are badly shaped for squared error. A proportion trained
directly on 0–1 can be predicted outside its own bounds, and squared error over a
proportion treats the difference between 0.01 and 0.02 as negligible when
epidemiologically it is a doubling. The logit fixes both. Case counts are non-negative
and heavily skewed, and `log1p` handles the zeros that a plain log would not.

`predict` inverts the transform by default, so prevalence comes back in $[0, 1]$ and
cases come back as counts. Passing `transformed=True` returns model space instead. That
is what you want when computing residuals or comparing against training targets, since
errors should be assessed on the scale the loss was defined on. It is almost never what
you want when plotting.

::: {.callout-note}
## The meaning of "state"

The *state* in `stateMINT` is the state of a **state-space model**, a hidden vector
carried through a linear recurrence that lets the network summarise everything it has
seen up to step $t$ in fixed memory. `d_state` 128 is the width of that vector.

It is **not** an epidemiological compartment. There is no susceptible, exposed, infected
or recovered class anywhere in the model. The emulator learned a mapping from covariates
to observed trajectories, and never represented the compartmental structure that
generated them. If you need S/I/R dynamics, you need the simulator, not the emulator.
:::
